simya.title: From alchemy to chemistry
simya.summary: Learn how alchemy, which did not measure, turned into chemistry, which measures and weighs.

cards.p: Alchemy (from Arabic al-kīmiyā) is the ancestor of chemistry. It also existed in China and India. Its Western branch passed from Alexandria to the Islamic world and from there to Europe. In alchemy, real experiments and magic went hand in hand.

once.soru: Alchemists tried to transform substances by heating and mixing them. Which science is this work the ancestor of today?

secenekler.neden: Curiosity about changing matter and lab experiments slowly turned into chemistry.
Astronomy grew out of watching the sky. Alchemy dealt with matter.
Alchemy studied how substances change, not living things.

cards.p: Alchemists searched for a legendary substance that would turn cheap metals like lead into gold. They called it the philosopher's stone. They tried for centuries, but never made a single gram of gold.

cards.p: The other dream was an elixir of life that would cure disease and extend life. It was never found, but the interest in preparing medicines helped pharmacy and medical chemistry grow.

once.soru: Alchemists searched for an elixir of life to cure disease. Which profession did this search help develop?

secenekler.neden: Mixing plants and minerals to prepare an elixir slowly fed into pharmacy and medical chemistry.
Architecture is about buildings. The search for an elixir led to preparing medicines.
The search for an elixir turned toward preparing medicines, not toward the sky.

cards.p: Alchemists developed tools such as the furnace, the mortar, the glass flask and the alembic. Jabir ibn Hayyan is credited with making nitric and sulfuric acid, and al-Razi with obtaining alcohol.

once.soru: Alchemists could not make gold. So what did they leave to us?

secenekler.neden: Tools like the furnace, mortar, glass flask and alembic, along with their experience in experiments, became the basis of the chemistry lab.
No alchemist ever made gold, because no such method exists.
They missed their goal, but their experiments and tools passed on to chemistry.

cards.p: Heating a liquid and cooling its vapor back into a liquid is called distillation. Substances separate because their boiling points differ. Alchemists developed this method, and today it is used to make perfume and fuel.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><path d='M50 60h14v25a28 28 0 1 1 -14 0z' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2'/><path d='M30 118A28 28 0 0 0 84 118Z' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.45'/><path d='M57 172q-10 -12 0 -24q10 12 0 24z' fill='var(--c2)'/><line x1='100' y1='61' x2='190' y2='95' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-opacity='0.3' stroke-width='14' fill='none'/><path d='M57 60V45L230 110' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><circle cx='231' cy='122' r='3' fill='var(--c1)'/><path d='M225 110v55h60v-55' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><rect x='226' y='146' width='58' height='18' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.45'/><text x='75' y='168' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>1 Heat</text><text x='72' y='38' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>2 It evaporates</text><text x='175' y='55' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>3 It cools and condenses</text><text x='255' y='185' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>4 Liquid is collected</text></svg>
cards.key: Distillation = evaporate + condense. It separates by boiling point difference.

cards.p: In his 1661 book The Sceptical Chymist, Robert Boyle questioned the idea of "four elements". He argued that every claim should be tested by experiment. For Boyle, a substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances is an element.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='simya-7' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='24' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Boyle's test: does it break down?</text><rect x='15' y='45' width='70' height='36' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c1)'/><text x='50' y='68' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Water</text><line x1='90' y1='63' x2='158' y2='63' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#simya-7)'/><text x='124' y='55' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>electrolysis</text><rect x='163' y='45' width='76' height='36' rx='8' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='201' y='68' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>H₂ + O₂</text><text x='282' y='68' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--c3)'>compound</text><rect x='15' y='120' width='70' height='36' rx='8' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c4)'/><text x='50' y='143' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Gold</text><line x1='90' y1='138' x2='158' y2='138' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#simya-7)'/><text x='124' y='130' font-size='11' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>any method</text><rect x='163' y='120' width='76' height='36' rx='8' fill='none' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><text x='201' y='143' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>no breakdown</text><text x='282' y='143' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--acc)'>element</text><text x='160' y='188' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>Element: a substance that cannot be broken into simpler ones</text></svg>
cards.key: If a substance breaks down into simpler substances, it is not an element.

cards.p: In a closed container the total mass does not change. This is called conservation of mass, and Lavoisier showed it in the 1770s. Burning is a substance combining with oxygen. This ended the idea that a substance called phlogiston leaves things as they burn.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='25' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>In a closed container, mass does not change</text><line x1='160' y1='60' x2='160' y2='170' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><rect x='120' y='170' width='80' height='8' fill='var(--muted)'/><line x1='60' y1='60' x2='260' y2='60' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='3' fill='none'/><path d='M152 60L160 48L168 60z' fill='var(--ink)'/><path d='M70 60L42 110M70 60L98 110M250 60L222 110M250 60L278 110' stroke='var(--muted)' fill='none'/><path d='M40 110h60a30 12 0 0 1 -60 0z' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)'/><path d='M220 110h60a30 12 0 0 1 -60 0z' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--ink)'/><circle cx='70' cy='96' r='12' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c1)'/><circle cx='250' cy='96' r='12' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.35' stroke='var(--c2)'/><text x='70' y='145' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Before: 100 g</text><text x='250' y='145' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>After: 100 g</text><text x='160' y='195' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>Lavoisier, late 18th century</text></svg>
cards.key: In an open container the mass can change. You only see conservation when you weigh everything.

cards.h: How did chemistry become a science?
cards.p: Alchemists hid what they knew and rarely measured. In chemistry, a claim is tested by experiment, and the result is measured and shared. The cycle of observation, hypothesis, experiment and conclusion is the scientific method.

etk.soru: Put each feature where it belongs: alchemy or chemistry as a science?
ogeler: Others could not repeat and check the experiments. This was a flaw of alchemy.
Lavoisier's precise weighing is the basis of modern chemistry.

cards.p:
• Alchemy searched for ways to transform matter and for the elixir of life, but failed.
• It left behind distillation and lab equipment.
• For Boyle, an element is a substance that cannot be broken into simpler substances.
• Lavoisier showed that mass is conserved in a closed container and that burning is combining with oxygen.
• Experiment and measurement are what made chemistry a science.

quiz.q: Match each name or experiment with what it gave to chemistry.
quiz.e: Al-Razi is credited with obtaining alcohol. Boyle defined the element by experiment, Lavoisier showed mass is conserved in a closed container, and electrolysis proved that water is a compound.

quiz.q: Apply Boyle's definition: put each substance in the right group.
ogeler: Water: breaks into H₂ and O₂
Oxygen: does not break into anything simpler
Limestone: gives lime and CO₂ when heated
Gold: does not break down in any way
Table salt: gives sodium and chlorine by electrolysis
Sulfur: does not break into anything simpler
quiz.e: Water, limestone and salt break down into simpler substances, so they are compounds. Oxygen, gold and sulfur do not break down by any chemical means, so they are elements.

quiz.q: Put the steps of the scientific method in order.
quiz.e: First you observe something, then you form a hypothesis that explains it. The hypothesis is tested by experiment, and a conclusion is drawn.

quiz.q: Acetone boils at 56 °C and water at 100 °C. If you distill an acetone–water mixture, which collects in the receiving flask first?
quiz.e: Acetone has the lower boiling point, so it evaporates first, condenses in the cooler and drips into the flask. Distillation separates by boiling point difference.
y: Water boils at a higher temperature. The substance with the lower boiling point evaporates first.
Their boiling points differ, so one evaporates first.
Distillation is used exactly to separate liquids with different boiling points.

kimya-bilimi.title: The language and safety of chemistry
kimya-bilimi.summary: Learn the fields of chemistry, symbols, formulas and the rules for working safely.

cards.p: Chemistry studies the structure, properties and changes of matter. Its branches are analytical, inorganic, organic, physical, bio-, polymer and industrial chemistry.

once.soru: A chemist measures how much of each substance a medicine contains. Which branch is this?

secenekler.neden: Analytical chemistry finds which substances are in a sample and in what amounts.
Polymer chemistry studies long-chain substances such as plastics.
Industrial chemistry deals with large-scale production. Measuring what a substance contains is the job of analytical chemistry.

cards.p: A chemical engineer designs processes in a plant, a metallurgical engineer works with metals, and a pharmacist prepares medicines and advises on doses. Medicine, food, paint and cosmetics all depend on chemistry.

once.soru: Who explains to a patient how and how much of a medicine to take?

secenekler.neden: A pharmacist prepares the medicine and explains its dose and use.
A chemical engineer designs production processes and does not give medicine to patients.
A metallurgical engineer works with metals and alloys.

cards.p: In a symbol the first letter is a capital and the second is lowercase (C, Ca, Co). Some symbols come from the element's Latin name. For example, the symbol for iron is Fe, for gold Au and for lead Pb. Berzelius proposed this system in 1813.

once.soru: Which one goes into the batter to make a cake rise?

secenekler.neden: Baking soda (NaHCO₃) gives off CO₂ gas when heated. These bubbles make the cake rise.
Caustic soda (NaOH) is a strong base and burns skin. It never goes into food.
Blue vitriol (copper sulfate) is toxic and used in farming. It never goes into food.

cards.p: In the lab you wear goggles, a lab coat and gloves. Acid is always added to water. Chemicals are never smelled or tasted. You do not eat in the lab, you do not pour waste down the sink, and you do not use unlabeled bottles.

cards.key: If a chemical splashes into your eye, rinse with plenty of water for at least 15 minutes and report it right away.

cards.p: The body needs some elements. Calcium works in bones, iron in hemoglobin, and sodium and potassium in nerve signals. Heavy metals such as mercury, lead and cadmium build up in the body and cause harm.

once.soru: Which element is in hemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood?

secenekler.neden: The iron in hemoglobin binds oxygen. Iron deficiency causes anemia.
Lead is a heavy metal that builds up in the body and causes harm.
Mercury is toxic and has no job in the body.

cards.p:
• Chemistry has branches and is used in many careers.
• In a symbol the first letter is a capital and the second is lowercase. The subscript in a formula shows the number of atoms.
• Compounds also have common names.
• Know the hazard symbols and follow the lab rules.
• Some elements are essential for the body, while heavy metals are harmful.

quiz.q: Match each substance with the hazard symbol you should see on its bottle.
quiz.e: Kerosene catches fire easily. Potassium nitrate gives off oxygen and makes burning more intense. Cyanide kills even in tiny amounts. Concentrated sulfuric acid eats away skin and metal.

quiz.q: Put each element in the right group.
quiz.e: Calcium works in bones and teeth, iron in hemoglobin, and sodium and potassium in nerve signals. Mercury, lead and cadmium build up in the body and damage organs.

quiz.q: How many atoms in total are in one H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> molecule?
quiz.e: Subscripts show the number of atoms. 2 H + 1 S + 4 O = 7 atoms. The subscript of S is 1, so it is not written.

quiz.q: What is the right way to dilute an acid?
o: Add the acid slowly to water
Pour water quickly onto the acid
Pour both into the container at once
Heat the acid, then add water
quiz.e: Acid is added slowly to water. If water is poured onto acid, the heat released boils the water and can splash the acid.
y: The first drops of water poured onto acid boil from the heat released and splash the acid. That is why acid is added slowly to water.
Pouring both at once does not stop the heat from being released out of control. Acid should be added to water a little at a time.
Heating the acid makes it more dangerous. Heat is released during dilution, so acid is added slowly to cold water.

madde.title: Matter and its properties
madde.summary: Everything around you is matter. Learn the states, types and changes of matter.

cards.p: Anything that has mass and takes up space is called matter. Water, air, stone and you are all matter. Light, sound and heat are not matter. They carry energy or are energy themselves.

cards.key: Anything with mass and volume is matter.

once.soru: Which one is not matter?

secenekler.neden: Light has no mass and takes up no space. Light only carries energy.
Air is a mixture of gases and has mass and volume. A blown-up balloon shows this.
Water vapor is water in the gas state, and it has mass and volume.

cards.p: In a solid, particles are packed tightly in order and vibrate in place. In a liquid, particles are close together but slide past each other. That is why a liquid takes the shape of its container. In a gas, particles are far apart and fast, and they fill the whole container.

cards.p: A substance that absorbs heat melts, evaporates, or goes straight from solid to gas, which is called sublimation. A substance that releases heat freezes, condenses, or goes straight from gas to solid, which is called deposition. In these changes the substance stays the same substance.

cards.p: An element is made of only one kind of atom (Fe, O₂) and cannot be broken into simpler substances. A compound forms when different atoms bond in a fixed ratio (H₂O), and it can be broken down by chemical means. Elements and compounds are both pure substances.

cards.key: O₂ is a molecule of an element, and H₂O is a molecule of a compound.

cards.p: In a mixture the substances keep their properties. A mixture that is the same everywhere, like sugar water, is homogeneous. One whose parts you can tell apart, like sandy water, is heterogeneous. Mixtures are separated by filtering or distillation.

cards.p: In a physical change the substance keeps its identity. In a chemical change a new substance forms. A change of color, gas given off, heat, light and a precipitate are clues of a chemical change. But boiling water also gives off gas.

etk.soru: Put each event in the right group: does the substance keep its identity, or does a new substance form?
ogeler: It is a change of state. Both ice and water are H₂O.
Sugar molecules spread through the water but do not change. When the water evaporates, the sugar is left behind.
Iron turns into iron oxide with oxygen and moisture.
Substances in the cut apple react with oxygen in the air.

cards.key: A physical change is often easy to reverse. A chemical change usually is not.

cards.p: Mass, volume and inertia belong to all matter, and they are called common properties. Density, melting and boiling point, and solubility are characteristic properties. You identify an unknown substance by these properties.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='14' y='14' width='140' height='172' rx='8' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='84' y='38' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Common</text><text x='84' y='66' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>mass</text><text x='84' y='90' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>volume</text><text x='84' y='114' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>inertia</text><text x='84' y='138' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>made of particles</text><text x='84' y='170' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>depends on amount</text><rect x='166' y='14' width='140' height='172' rx='8' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--acc)' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='236' y='38' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Characteristic</text><text x='236' y='64' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>density</text><text x='236' y='86' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>melting point</text><text x='236' y='108' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>boiling point</text><text x='236' y='130' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>solubility</text><text x='236' y='152' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>conductivity</text><text x='236' y='170' font-size='10' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>identifies the substance</text></svg>
cards.key: 10 g of water and 100 g of water have the same density but different masses.

once.soru: Two bottles have lost their labels, and both hold a colorless liquid. Which measurement tells you which one is water?

secenekler.neden: Pure water boils at 100 °C at 1 atm. Boiling point is a characteristic property that identifies a substance.
Every substance has mass, and it depends on the amount. So it does not identify the substance.
Volume depends on the amount. Different liquids can have the same volume.

cards.p: Mass per unit volume is called density, and it is calculated with d = m / V. At the same temperature and pressure, every pure substance has a fixed density that identifies it. A substance less dense than water floats on it.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='100' y='30' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>d = m / V</text><rect x='31' y='80' width='138' height='89' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25'/><path d='M30 50v120h140v-120' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'/><rect x='50' y='78' width='34' height='26' rx='3' fill='var(--panel)' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2'/><rect x='120' y='150' width='30' height='18' fill='var(--muted)'/><line x1='86' y1='90' x2='182' y2='90' stroke='var(--line)' fill='none'/><line x1='170' y1='125' x2='182' y2='125' stroke='var(--line)' fill='none'/><line x1='152' y1='160' x2='182' y2='160' stroke='var(--line)' fill='none'/><text x='186' y='94' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>ice 0.92 g/cm³</text><text x='186' y='129' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>water 1.00 g/cm³</text><text x='186' y='164' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>iron 7.87 g/cm³</text><text x='186' y='188' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>less dense floats</text></svg>

etk.soru: d = m / V. Change the mass and volume: does the object float or sink in water? (Water: 1.00 g/cm³)
yorum: This substance is less dense than water and floats.
This substance has the same density as water and stays suspended in it.
This substance is denser than water and sinks.

cards.key: d = m / V  (water ≈ 1 g/cm³; ice ≈ 0.92 g/cm³. Iron ≈ 7.87 g/cm³)

once.soru: Ice floats on water. How does the density of ice compare with water's?

secenekler.neden: A substance less dense than water floats. Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³, and water about 1 g/cm³.
If it were denser than water, it would sink.
If they were equal, it would stay suspended in the water.

cards.p:
• Matter is anything with mass and volume, and it has three states.
• An element does not break down, while a compound breaks into its elements by chemical means.
• Mixtures can be homogeneous or heterogeneous.
• In a physical change the identity stays the same. In a chemical change a new substance forms.
• Density, melting point and boiling point identify a substance.

quiz.q: Put each event in the right group.
quiz.e: In melting, sublimation, fogging (condensation) and dissolving, the substance stays the same. A burning candle gives CO₂ and water. In a cooking egg the proteins permanently lose their shape (denaturation) and link together. Tarnished silver forms silver sulfide.

quiz.q: Match each change of state with its name.
quiz.e: A solid melts when it turns into a liquid. A liquid freezes when it turns into a solid and evaporates when it turns into a gas. A solid turning straight into a gas is sublimation, and the reverse is deposition.

quiz.q: A substance has a mass of 54 g and a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density in g/cm³?
quiz.e: Density is mass per unit volume. d = m / V = 54 / 20 = 2.7 g/cm³. This is the density of aluminum.

quiz.q: Which one is a compound?
quiz.e: H₂O forms from different atoms bonded in a fixed ratio, and electrolysis splits it into H₂ and O₂.
y: O₂ is a molecule with two atoms, but both atoms are oxygen. So it is a molecule of an element.
In salt water, salt and water mix without bonding to each other. It is a mixture whose ratio can vary.
Fe is made of one kind of atom and cannot be broken into simpler substances. So it is an element.

atom-modelleri.title: The history of atomic models
atom-modelleri.summary: How were atomic models built to explain experimental results, and how did they develop?

olay.h: The gold foil that changed the model of the atom
olay.p: Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at a very thin gold foil. What they saw could not be explained by the atomic model of the day. In this lesson you will do the same experiment.

cards.p: An atom is too small to see, even with a microscope. Scientists built models that explain experimental results. When a new experiment could not be explained, the model changed.

etk.soru: Put the atomic models in the order they appeared, from oldest to newest.

cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='atom-modelleri-1' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--muted)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='25' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Timeline of atomic models</text><line x1='12' y1='100' x2='312' y2='100' stroke='var(--muted)' stroke-width='3' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-1)'/><circle cx='40' cy='100' r='7' fill='var(--muted)'/><circle cx='90' cy='100' r='7' fill='var(--c4)'/><circle cx='145' cy='100' r='7' fill='var(--c2)'/><circle cx='195' cy='100' r='7' fill='var(--c3)'/><circle cx='250' cy='100' r='7' fill='var(--c5)'/><circle cx='290' cy='100' r='7' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='40' y='70' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Democritus</text><text x='40' y='86' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>~400 BCE</text><text x='90' y='126' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Dalton</text><text x='90' y='142' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>1803</text><text x='145' y='70' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Thomson</text><text x='145' y='86' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>1904</text><text x='195' y='126' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Rutherford</text><text x='195' y='142' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>1911</text><text x='250' y='70' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Bohr</text><text x='250' y='86' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>1913</text><text x='290' y='126' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Modern</text><text x='290' y='142' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>1926</text><text x='160' y='182' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--acc)'>New experiment → new model</text></svg>

once.soru: You cannot see inside a closed box. How can you find out what is in it?

secenekler.neden: When you cannot see, you experiment and build a model from the results. This is how scientists studied the atom.
Even if you cannot see inside, experiments can tell you what is there.
A guess with no experiment behind it cannot be tested. A model must rest on experimental results.

cards.p: Democritus (5th century BCE) said that if you keep dividing matter, you finally reach particles that cannot be divided. He called them atomos. This was a philosophical idea, not an experiment, and it was not accepted for centuries.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='atom-modelleri-2' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><text x='160' y='30' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Divide, divide, divide... and then?</text><rect x='15' y='60' width='70' height='70' rx='4' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--muted)'/><line x1='92' y1='95' x2='118' y2='95' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-2)'/><rect x='125' y='72' width='22' height='46' rx='3' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--muted)'/><rect x='151' y='72' width='22' height='46' rx='3' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--muted)'/><line x1='180' y1='95' x2='206' y2='95' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-2)'/><rect x='213' y='83' width='10' height='10' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.4'/><rect x='227' y='83' width='10' height='10' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.4'/><rect x='213' y='97' width='10' height='10' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.4'/><rect x='227' y='97' width='10' height='10' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.4'/><line x1='245' y1='95' x2='271' y2='95' stroke='var(--ink)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-2)'/><circle cx='287' cy='95' r='5' fill='var(--acc)'/><text x='287' y='125' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>atomos</text><text x='287' y='141' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>indivisible</text><text x='160' y='180' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>Only thought, no experiment</text></svg>

once.soru: You cut a piece of gold in half, then in half again. Can you keep doing this forever?

secenekler.neden: In the end you reach the smallest piece of gold, a gold atom. Democritus thought the same and called this particle atomos.
Matter cannot be divided forever. In the end you reach an atom.
The gold does not vanish. The smallest piece of gold is a gold atom.

cards.p: Dalton (1803) pictured atoms as solid spheres that cannot be divided. In his view, atoms of the same element are identical and combine in compounds in a fixed ratio. Once electrons and isotopes were found, this model was no longer enough.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='30' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Solid, indivisible spheres</text><g fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.8'><circle cx='35' cy='85' r='12'/><circle cx='65' cy='85' r='12'/><circle cx='50' cy='112' r='12'/><circle cx='243' cy='112' r='12'/><circle cx='277' cy='112' r='12'/></g><g fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.8'><circle cx='130' cy='82' r='16'/><circle cx='166' cy='82' r='16'/><circle cx='148' cy='112' r='16'/><circle cx='260' cy='92' r='16'/></g><g fill='var(--panel)' fill-opacity='0.6'><circle cx='31' cy='81' r='3'/><circle cx='61' cy='81' r='3'/><circle cx='46' cy='108' r='3'/><circle cx='125' cy='77' r='4'/><circle cx='161' cy='77' r='4'/><circle cx='143' cy='107' r='4'/><circle cx='255' cy='87' r='4'/></g><text x='50' y='148' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>H atoms are identical</text><text x='148' y='148' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>O atoms are identical</text><text x='260' y='148' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Water: 2 H + 1 O</text><text x='160' y='182' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>Explained: conservation of mass, fixed ratios</text></svg>

once.soru: Water always forms in a ratio of 1 gram of hydrogen to 8 grams of oxygen. How did Dalton explain this?

secenekler.neden: Every water molecule has the same number of H and O atoms. That is why the mass ratio is always the same.
The ratio comes out the same every time. If it were random, it would vary.
In Dalton's view, atoms do not turn into other atoms.

cards.key: Atoms of the same element with different masses are called isotopes. You will see isotopes in the topic on the structure of the atom.

cards.p: In 1897 Thomson showed that cathode (negative terminal) rays are made of negatively charged electrons. In his model the atom was a positively charged sphere with electrons embedded in it like raisins.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><circle cx='110' cy='105' r='75' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.18' stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2'/><g font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--c2)'><text x='110' y='58'>+</text><text x='55' y='105'>+</text><text x='170' y='95'>+</text><text x='100' y='155'>+</text><text x='150' y='168'>+</text><text x='85' y='110'>+</text><text x='60' y='150'>+</text></g><g fill='var(--c1)'><circle cx='80' cy='70' r='9'/><circle cx='140' cy='72' r='9'/><circle cx='70' cy='128' r='9'/><circle cx='135' cy='140' r='9'/><circle cx='112' cy='103' r='9'/><circle cx='162' cy='120' r='9'/></g><g font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--panel)'><text x='80' y='74'>−</text><text x='140' y='76'>−</text><text x='70' y='132'>−</text><text x='135' y='144'>−</text><text x='112' y='107'>−</text><text x='162' y='124'>−</text></g><text x='200' y='70' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)'>positive sphere (+)</text><text x='200' y='110' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)'>electrons (−)</text><text x='200' y='150' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)'>total charge: 0</text></svg>

cards.h: Millikan: the charge of the electron
cards.p: In 1909 Millikan held charged oil droplets suspended between two plates. The charges he measured always came out as whole multiples of 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C. This value is the charge of one electron.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='atom-modelleri-m1' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--c3)'/></marker><marker id='atom-modelleri-m2' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--c4)'/></marker></defs><rect x='16' y='36' width='160' height='9' rx='2' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.55'/><rect x='16' y='160' width='160' height='9' rx='2' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.55'/><g font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='36' y='30'>+</text><text x='76' y='30'>+</text><text x='116' y='30'>+</text><text x='156' y='30'>+</text></g><g font-size='14' fill='var(--c1)' text-anchor='middle'><text x='36' y='186'>−</text><text x='76' y='186'>−</text><text x='116' y='186'>−</text><text x='156' y='186'>−</text></g><circle cx='70' cy='103' r='8' fill='var(--c4)'/><text x='70' y='107' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700' fill='var(--panel)'>−</text><line x1='70' y1='93' x2='70' y2='58' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-m1)'/><line x1='70' y1='113' x2='70' y2='148' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2.5' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-m2)'/><text x='80' y='72' font-size='11' fill='var(--c3)'>electric force</text><text x='80' y='140' font-size='11' fill='var(--c4)'>weight</text><text x='196' y='60' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>The drop stays still:</text><text x='196' y='78' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>the two forces are equal</text><text x='196' y='116' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>Charge is always a</text><text x='196' y='132' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>whole multiple of e:</text><text x='196' y='158' font-size='13' font-weight='700' fill='var(--c1)'>e = 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C</text></svg>
cards.key: Charge is quantized. Every charge is a whole multiple of the electron's charge.

once.soru: The charge of oil drops is measured. The results always come out as 1, 2, 3... times 1.6·10⁻¹⁹ C. What does this show?

secenekler.neden: The smallest piece of charge is the charge of one electron, and every charge is a whole multiple of it.
Measurement errors would scatter the results at random. Getting whole multiples every time is a rule.
No values in between ever showed up, because charge is quantized.

cards.p: This result could not be explained by Thomson's model, because positive charge spread everywhere could not turn an alpha particle back. Rutherford described it like this: "You fire a shell at a sheet of tissue paper, and it comes back."
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='atom-modelleri-5' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--c2)'/></marker></defs><path d='M157 10A90 90 0 0 1 157 190' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5 4' fill='none'/><rect x='8' y='85' width='50' height='30' rx='4' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--muted)'/><text x='33' y='135' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>α source</text><rect x='155' y='50' width='5' height='100' fill='var(--c4)'/><text x='157' y='170' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>gold foil</text><g stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'><line x1='58' y1='100' x2='150' y2='100' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-5)'/><line x1='160' y1='94' x2='238' y2='94' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-5)'/><line x1='160' y1='106' x2='238' y2='106' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-5)'/><line x1='160' y1='100' x2='212' y2='58' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-5)'/><line x1='160' y1='100' x2='212' y2='142' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-5)'/><line x1='153' y1='98' x2='100' y2='72' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-5)'/></g><text x='8' y='25' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>→ most went straight through</text><text x='8' y='42' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>↗ some were deflected</text><text x='8' y='59' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>↩ very few bounced back</text><text x='252' y='104' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>screen</text></svg>

cards.p: For Rutherford (1911), since most particles passed through the foil, the atom must be mostly empty space. The positive charge and the mass are packed into a very small nucleus. The electrons move around this nucleus.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='atom-modelleri-6' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--c2)'/></marker></defs><circle cx='170' cy='60' r='38' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><circle cx='170' cy='140' r='38' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.06' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'/><circle cx='170' cy='60' r='4' fill='var(--c2)'/><circle cx='170' cy='140' r='4' fill='var(--c2)'/><g stroke='var(--c2)' stroke-width='2' fill='none'><path d='M20 34H295' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-6)'/><path d='M20 130H150Q172 126 290 84' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-6)'/><path d='M20 60H158Q164 62 158 66L40 88' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-6)'/></g><line x1='174' y1='143' x2='212' y2='166' stroke='var(--ink)' fill='none'/><text x='215' y='172' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>nucleus (+)</text><text x='300' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>empty space: goes straight</text><text x='300' y='75' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='end'>close: deflected</text><text x='20' y='110' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>very close: pushed back</text></svg>
cards.key: This model had a problem. An orbiting electron should give off energy and fall into the nucleus.

cards.p: In 1919 Rutherford found the positive particle in the nucleus, the proton. But the mass of nuclei was more than the protons could account for. In 1932 Chadwick found the uncharged neutron.

once.soru: A helium nucleus has 2 protons, but its mass is close to 4 protons. Where does the extra mass come from?

secenekler.neden: The nucleus also holds uncharged neutrons. Because they have no charge, they were found last, in 1932.
An electron is about 1836 times lighter than a proton. So it cannot explain the difference.
The difference showed up regularly in every nucleus. So it was something real.

cards.p: For Bohr (1913), electrons move only in certain energy levels and lose no energy there. When an electron drops to a lower level, it gives off light of a certain color. But this model worked only for particles with a single electron.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='atom-modelleri-7' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--c1)'/></marker><marker id='atom-modelleri-7b' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--c4)'/></marker></defs><circle cx='110' cy='100' r='30' fill='none' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='110' cy='100' r='55' fill='none' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='110' cy='100' r='80' fill='none' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='110' cy='100' r='8' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='110' y='67' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>n=1</text><text x='110' y='42' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>n=2</text><text x='110' y='17' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>n=3</text><circle cx='179' cy='60' r='5' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.35'/><circle cx='158' cy='72' r='5' fill='var(--c1)'/><line x1='175' y1='62' x2='163' y2='69' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-7)'/><path d='M178 92q6 -8 12 0t12 0t12 0t12 0' stroke='var(--c4)' stroke-width='2' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atom-modelleri-7b)'/><text x='232' y='96' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>gives off light</text><text x='200' y='150' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>n: energy level</text><text x='200' y='168' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)'>(shell)</text></svg>
cards.key: An electron absorbs energy when it moves up a level and gives it off as light when it drops down.

cards.h: The modern model: the electron cloud
cards.p: In the modern model there is no exact orbit. Quantum mechanics only lets us calculate the probability of finding the electron in a region. These regions are called orbitals.

• Democritus put forward the idea of the indivisible atomos.
• Dalton pictured the atom as a solid sphere. Thomson found the electron, and Millikan measured its charge.
• Rutherford found the small, positive nucleus. The atom is mostly empty space.
• Bohr proposed energy levels. The modern model describes orbitals.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='30' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>The model changed with experiments</text><circle cx='32' cy='90' r='24' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.5'/><circle cx='94' cy='90' r='24' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c2)'/><g fill='var(--c1)'><circle cx='86' cy='80' r='3'/><circle cx='103' cy='84' r='3'/><circle cx='88' cy='100' r='3'/><circle cx='102' cy='99' r='3'/></g><circle cx='156' cy='90' r='24' fill='none' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='3 2'/><circle cx='156' cy='90' r='3' fill='var(--c2)'/><circle cx='174' cy='80' r='3' fill='var(--c1)'/><circle cx='140' cy='104' r='3' fill='var(--c1)'/><circle cx='218' cy='90' r='12' fill='none' stroke='var(--line)'/><circle cx='218' cy='90' r='22' fill='none' stroke='var(--line)'/><circle cx='218' cy='90' r='3' fill='var(--c2)'/><circle cx='230' cy='90' r='3' fill='var(--c1)'/><circle cx='218' cy='68' r='3' fill='var(--c1)'/><g fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.15'><circle cx='280' cy='90' r='24'/><circle cx='280' cy='90' r='16'/><circle cx='280' cy='90' r='9'/></g><circle cx='280' cy='90' r='3' fill='var(--c2)'/><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='32' y='135'>Dalton</text><text x='94' y='135'>Thomson</text><text x='156' y='135'>Rutherford</text><text x='218' y='135'>Bohr</text><text x='280' y='135'>Cloud</text></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'><text x='32' y='152'>1803</text><text x='94' y='152'>1904</text><text x='156' y='152'>1911</text><text x='218' y='152'>1913</text><text x='280' y='152'>1926</text></g></svg>

quiz.q: Match each experiment or observation with the model it showed to be incomplete.
ciftler: Particles bouncing back from gold foil
quiz.e: The electron showed that the atom can be divided, which left Dalton's model incomplete. Particles bouncing back revealed the small nucleus, which left Thomson's model incomplete. Rutherford could not explain the line spectrum. Bohr's model failed for many-electron atoms.

quiz.q: Match each experiment or finding with the scientist.
ciftler: Discovering the electron with cathode rays
quiz.e: Thomson found the electron with cathode rays, and Millikan measured its charge with oil drops. The gold foil experiment was done under Rutherford's direction, Chadwick found the neutron, and Bohr explained the hydrogen spectrum.

quiz.q: Sort each model by whether the atom has a nucleus.
quiz.e: Dalton thought of the atom as a solid sphere, and Thomson as electrons embedded in a positive sphere. Neither had the idea of a nucleus. Rutherford found the nucleus. Bohr's model and the modern model describe the electrons around the nucleus.

quiz.q: In the gold foil experiment, what does it show that a few alpha particles bounced back?
o: Most of the atom is empty space
Mass and positive charge are packed into a tiny nucleus
Positive charge is spread evenly through the atom
quiz.e: To bounce back, a particle must meet a very strong push. That only happens if the positive charge and mass are packed into a very small volume.
y: Most particles go straight through the empty space. Bouncing back points to a strong push.
Electrons are negatively charged and much lighter than an alpha particle. So they cannot turn it back.
Spread-out positive charge, as in Thomson's model, pushes only weakly. It cannot turn a fast alpha particle back.

atomun-yapisi.title: The structure of the atom
atomun-yapisi.summary: Learn what is inside an atom: protons, neutrons, electrons and how they are arranged.

cards.p: An atom is made of three particles. The proton has a charge of +1, the neutron has no charge, and the electron has a charge of −1. A proton and a neutron each have a mass of about 1 amu. An electron is 1836 times lighter than a proton.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><g font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'><text x='55' y='40'>Particle</text><text x='140' y='40'>Charge</text><text x='200' y='40'>Mass (amu)</text><text x='275' y='40'>Location</text></g><line x1='10' y1='52' x2='310' y2='52' stroke='var(--line)' fill='none'/><line x1='10' y1='98' x2='310' y2='98' stroke='var(--line)' fill='none'/><line x1='10' y1='138' x2='310' y2='138' stroke='var(--line)' fill='none'/><circle cx='25' cy='75' r='9' fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.7'/><circle cx='25' cy='118' r='9' fill='var(--muted)' fill-opacity='0.7'/><circle cx='25' cy='160' r='5' fill='var(--c1)'/><g font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='42' y='80'>Proton</text><text x='42' y='123'>Neutron</text><text x='42' y='165'>Electron</text></g><g font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='140' y='80'>+1</text><text x='140' y='123'>0</text><text x='140' y='165'>−1</text><text x='200' y='80'>≈ 1</text><text x='200' y='123'>≈ 1</text><text x='200' y='165'>≈ 0.0005</text><text x='275' y='80'>nucleus</text><text x='275' y='123'>nucleus</text><text x='275' y='165'>shells</text></g></svg>
cards.key: The charges of a proton and an electron are equal in size but opposite in sign. amu stands for atomic mass unit.

cards.p: The nucleus, where the protons and neutrons are, is 10 000 to 100 000 times smaller than the atom, but more than 99.9% of the mass is there.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><ellipse cx='160' cy='105' rx='140' ry='60' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--c3)' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='160' cy='105' rx='95' ry='36' fill='none' stroke='var(--line)'/><circle cx='160' cy='105' r='2.5' fill='var(--c2)'/><line x1='162' y1='103' x2='200' y2='38' stroke='var(--ink)' fill='none'/><text x='304' y='30' font-size='12' text-anchor='end' fill='var(--ink)'>nucleus = a pea</text><text x='20' y='30' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>atom = a stadium</text><text x='160' y='188' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>The atom's diameter is ~10⁴–10⁵ times the nucleus's</text></svg>
cards.key: The rest of the atom is the empty space where the electrons are.

cards.p: The number of protons in an atom is its atomic number (Z), and it decides what the atom is. Every atom with 6 protons is carbon, and every atom with 8 protons is oxygen.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='28' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Number of protons = identity</text><g fill='none' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'><circle cx='55' cy='92' r='35'/><circle cx='160' cy='92' r='35'/><circle cx='265' cy='92' r='35'/></g><g fill='var(--c2)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c2)'><circle cx='55' cy='92' r='18'/><circle cx='160' cy='92' r='18'/><circle cx='265' cy='92' r='18'/></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='55' y='96'>1p</text><text x='160' y='96'>6p</text><text x='265' y='96'>8p</text></g><g font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='55' y='150'>Z = 1</text><text x='160' y='150'>Z = 6</text><text x='265' y='150'>Z = 8</text></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'><text x='55' y='170'>Hydrogen</text><text x='160' y='170'>Carbon</text><text x='265' y='170'>Oxygen</text></g></svg>
cards.key: Z = number of protons (in a neutral atom, the number of electrons is also Z)

cards.p: The total number of protons and neutrons is the mass number (A). A is written at the upper left of the symbol, and Z at the lower left. For example, the atom 2311Na has 12 neutrons.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='25' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Sodium atom</text><g transform='translate(20,40) scale(2)'><text x='0' y='18' font-size='12' fill='var(--c1)'>23</text><text x='0' y='44' font-size='12' fill='var(--c2)'>11</text><text x='17' y='36' font-size='15' fill='var(--ink)'>Na</text></g><line x1='70' y1='68' x2='132' y2='66' stroke='var(--c1)' fill='none'/><line x1='70' y1='122' x2='132' y2='127' stroke='var(--c2)' fill='none'/><line x1='100' y1='100' x2='132' y2='97' stroke='var(--muted)' fill='none'/><text x='138' y='70' font-size='13' fill='var(--c1)'>A = 23 (p + n)</text><text x='138' y='101' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)'>Na: symbol</text><text x='138' y='131' font-size='13' fill='var(--c2)'>Z = 11 (protons)</text><rect x='130' y='150' width='180' height='28' rx='6' fill='var(--acc)' fill-opacity='0.15' stroke='var(--acc)'/><text x='220' y='169' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>p = 11, n = 12, e = 11</text></svg>
cards.key: Since A = p + n, the number of neutrons is A − Z.

once.soru: An atom has 6 protons and 8 neutrons. About how many amu is its mass?

secenekler.neden: A proton and a neutron are each about 1 amu, and electrons have almost no mass. So 6 + 8 = 14. This number is called the mass number.
6 is only what the protons add. Each neutron also adds about 1 amu.
You counted only the neutrons. Each proton also adds 1 amu.

cards.p: Atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. Their chemical properties are the same, but properties that depend on mass, such as density, are different.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><circle cx='20' cy='20' r='6' fill='var(--c2)'/><text x='30' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>proton</text><circle cx='90' cy='20' r='6' fill='var(--muted)'/><text x='100' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>neutron</text><circle cx='170' cy='20' r='4' fill='var(--c1)'/><text x='180' y='24' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'>electron</text><g fill='none' stroke='var(--line)' stroke-dasharray='4 3'><circle cx='55' cy='95' r='35'/><circle cx='160' cy='95' r='35'/><circle cx='265' cy='95' r='35'/></g><g fill='var(--c1)'><circle cx='55' cy='60' r='4'/><circle cx='160' cy='60' r='4'/><circle cx='265' cy='60' r='4'/></g><g fill='var(--c2)'><circle cx='55' cy='95' r='8'/><circle cx='153' cy='95' r='8'/><circle cx='265' cy='88' r='8'/></g><g fill='var(--muted)'><circle cx='167' cy='95' r='8'/><circle cx='257' cy='102' r='8'/><circle cx='273' cy='102' r='8'/></g><g font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='55' y='150'>¹H</text><text x='160' y='150'>²H</text><text x='265' y='150'>³H</text></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='55' y='168'>hydrogen</text><text x='160' y='168'>deuterium</text><text x='265' y='168'>tritium</text></g><g font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'><text x='55' y='186'>0 neutrons</text><text x='160' y='186'>1 neutron</text><text x='265' y='186'>2 neutrons</text></g></svg>
cards.key: Neutral isotopes also have the same number of electrons. The isotopes of hydrogen are <sup>1</sup>H, <sup>2</sup>H (deuterium) and <sup>3</sup>H (tritium).

cards.p: An atom that gives up or gains electrons becomes an ion. An atom that gives up electrons becomes a positive cation (Na+), and an atom that gains electrons becomes a negative anion (Cl−). The number of protons does not change.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><defs><marker id='atomun-yapisi-6' viewBox='0 0 10 10' refX='9' refY='5' markerWidth='6' markerHeight='6' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0L10 5L0 10z' fill='var(--ink)'/></marker></defs><circle cx='60' cy='60' r='28' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c4)'/><text x='60' y='58' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Na</text><text x='60' y='75' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>11p 11e</text><circle cx='260' cy='60' r='28' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='260' y='58' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Cl</text><text x='260' y='75' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>17p 17e</text><line x1='95' y1='60' x2='225' y2='60' stroke='var(--c1)' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5 3' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atomun-yapisi-6)'/><text x='160' y='50' font-size='13' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--c1)'>1 e⁻</text><line x1='60' y1='92' x2='60' y2='116' stroke='var(--ink)' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atomun-yapisi-6)'/><line x1='260' y1='92' x2='260' y2='108' stroke='var(--ink)' fill='none' marker-end='url(#atomun-yapisi-6)'/><circle cx='60' cy='145' r='24' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c4)'/><text x='60' y='143' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Na⁺</text><text x='60' y='159' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>11p 10e</text><circle cx='260' cy='145' r='32' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='260' y='143' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Cl⁻</text><text x='260' y='159' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>17p 18e</text><text x='60' y='192' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>cation (+)</text><text x='260' y='192' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>anion (−)</text></svg>
cards.key: The charge of an ion is the number of protons minus the number of electrons.

cards.p: Atoms with the same number of neutrons are called isotones (¹⁴C, ¹⁶O). Atoms with the same mass number are called isobars (¹⁴C, ¹⁴N). These atoms belong to different elements.

etk.soru: Match each pair of particles with the right name, based on the number they share.

cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><g font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)'><text x='70' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Name</text><text x='165' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Same</text><text x='262' y='26' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Example</text><line x1='14' y1='36' x2='306' y2='36' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='70' y='58' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Isotope</text><text x='165' y='58' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle'>protons (Z)</text><text x='262' y='58' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>¹²C, ¹⁴C</text><line x1='14' y1='74' x2='306' y2='74' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='70' y='96' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Isotone</text><text x='165' y='96' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle'>neutrons</text><text x='262' y='96' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>¹⁴C, ¹⁶O</text><line x1='14' y1='112' x2='306' y2='112' stroke='var(--line)'/><text x='70' y='134' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>Isobar</text><text x='165' y='134' font-size='12' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle'>mass no. (A)</text><text x='262' y='134' font-size='12' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle'>¹⁴C, ¹⁴N</text></g><text x='160' y='176' font-size='12' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>only isotopes are the same element</text></svg>
cards.key: Atoms with the same number of protons are isotopes. Only isotopes belong to the same element.

once.soru: What do the atoms ¹⁴C and ¹⁶O have in common? (C: 6, O: 8 protons)

secenekler.neden: ¹⁴C has 14 − 6 = 8 neutrons, and ¹⁶O has 16 − 8 = 8. Atoms with the same number of neutrons are called isotones.
Carbon has 6 protons and oxygen 8. If they had the same number of protons, they would be the same element.
The mass numbers are written at the upper left of the symbol, and they are 14 and 16.

cards.p: Particles with the same number of electrons are called isoelectronic. To count, start from the neutral atom. For a cation, subtract as many electrons as its charge. For an anion, add as many electrons as its charge.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><text x='160' y='26' font-size='14' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>All have 10 electrons</text><circle cx='60' cy='92' r='34' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c4)'/><text x='60' y='90' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Na⁺</text><text x='60' y='108' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>11p 10e</text><circle cx='160' cy='92' r='34' fill='var(--c5)' fill-opacity='0.2' stroke='var(--c5)'/><text x='160' y='90' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>Ne</text><text x='160' y='108' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>10p 10e</text><circle cx='260' cy='92' r='34' fill='var(--c3)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c3)'/><text x='260' y='90' font-size='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>F⁻</text><text x='260' y='108' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--muted)'>9p 10e</text><text x='60' y='150' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>11 − 1 = 10</text><text x='160' y='150' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>10</text><text x='260' y='150' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--ink)'>9 + 1 = 10</text><text x='160' y='186' font-size='12' text-anchor='middle' fill='var(--acc)'>number of electrons = Z − ion charge</text></svg>
cards.key: Mg²⁺, Na⁺, Ne, F⁻ and O²⁻ all have 10 electrons.

once.soru: How many electrons does the Na⁺ ion have? (Na: 11 protons)

secenekler.neden: Neutral sodium has 11 electrons. The + charge shows that sodium gave up one electron, so 11 − 1 = 10. The Ne atom also has 10 electrons.
11 is the number of electrons in neutral sodium. Think about what the + charge tells you.
A cation is a particle that gives up electrons, not one that gains them.

cards.p: The atomic mass in the periodic table is an average based on how common each isotope is in nature. That is why it is not a whole number.
cards.svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 200'><rect x='30' y='40' width='180' height='34' rx='6' fill='var(--c1)' fill-opacity='0.25' stroke='var(--c1)'/><rect x='210' y='40' width='60' height='34' rx='6' fill='var(--c4)' fill-opacity='0.3' stroke='var(--c4)'/><text x='120' y='62' font-size='13' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>³⁵Cl  75%</text><text x='240' y='62' font-size='11' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>³⁷Cl 25%</text><text x='160' y='112' font-size='15' fill='var(--ink)' text-anchor='middle' font-weight='700'>0.75·35 + 0.25·37 ≈ 35.5</text><text x='160' y='136' font-size='11' fill='var(--muted)' text-anchor='middle'>atomic mass in the table = average by abundance</text><text x='160' y='170' font-size='11' fill='var(--acc)' text-anchor='middle'>mass number (A): p + n count of a single atom</text></svg>
cards.key: The mass number is always a whole number. The average atomic mass can be a decimal.

once.soru: 75% of chlorine atoms are ³⁵Cl and 25% are ³⁷Cl. What is the average atomic mass of chlorine?

secenekler.neden: The more common isotope counts more. 0.75 · 35 + 0.25 · 37 = 35.5.
36 is the plain average of the two masses. But ³⁵Cl is three times more common.
The average comes out close to the more common isotope. Check which one is more common.

cards.p: Electrons are arranged in shells around the nucleus. For the first 20 elements, the 1st shell holds at most 2 electrons, and the 2nd and 3rd shells hold at most 8 each.

cards.key: Na (11 electrons) is arranged 2-8-1, and Ca (20 electrons) 2-8-8-2. You will see why the 3rd shell stops at 8 in the topic on modern atomic theory.

cards.p: The electrons in the outermost shell are valence electrons. Atoms tend to complete their outer shell to 8 (2 for the very small ones), like the noble gases (gases such as He, Ne and Ar that do not react).

cards.key: That is why Na gives up 1 electron and Cl gains 1 electron.

cards.p:
• Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus, and electrons are around it.
• Z is the number of protons, and A is the total number of protons and neutrons.
• Isotopes share Z, isotones share the number of neutrons, isobars share A, and isoelectronic particles share the number of electrons.
• An ion is an atom that has gained or given up electrons.
• For the first 20 elements, shells fill as 2-8-8.

quiz.q: Magnesium has atomic number 12. How many electrons are in the Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion?
quiz.e: A neutral Mg atom has 12 electrons. After giving up 2 electrons, 12 − 2 = 10 electrons are left.

quiz.q: Put each pair of atoms in the right group. (Z: H 1, He 2, C 6, N 7, O 8, Na 11, Mg 12, Ar 18, Ca 20)
quiz.e: Isotopes share the number of protons, and isobars share the mass number. Isotones share the number of neutrons. <sup>13</sup>C and <sup>14</sup>N have 7 neutrons, and <sup>23</sup>Na and <sup>24</sup>Mg have 12.

quiz.q: Use the counters to build the <sup>37</sup>Cl<sup>−</sup> ion. (Cl: Z = 17)
quiz.e: Since Z = 17, the atom has 17 protons. The number of neutrons is A − Z = 37 − 17 = 20. The charge is −1, so there is one extra electron, giving 18 electrons.

quiz.q: In nature, 20% of boron atoms are <sup>10</sup>B and 80% are <sup>11</sup>B. What is the average atomic mass of boron, approximately?
quiz.e: The average is weighted by abundance. 0.20 · 10 + 0.80 · 11 = 2 + 8.8 = 10.8. The heavier isotope is more common, so the result is close to 11.

modern-atom-teorisi.title: Modern atomic theory
modern-atom-teorisi.summary: Orbitals, quantum numbers and how electrons are arranged in an atom.

cards.p: According to de Broglie, an electron also behaves like a wave. According to Heisenberg, an electron's position and speed cannot both be known exactly at the same time. So Schrödinger gave the electron an orbital instead of a path. An orbital is a region where the electron is likely to be found.

once.soru: Can we measure both the position and the speed of an electron exactly at the same time?

secenekler.neden: According to Heisenberg, the more exactly the position is known, the less certain the speed becomes. So an electron is given a region of probability, not a path.
The problem is not the instruments but nature itself. A better instrument does not remove this uncertainty.

secenekler.yazi: Only when it is at rest
secenekler.neden: An electron is never at rest. Its position and speed never become certain together.

cards.p: Four quantum numbers give each electron's address. n gives the shell, ℓ the subshell and its shape, mℓ the orientation, and ms the spin. The first three describe the orbital, and the fourth describes the electron.

once.soru: A home address is given by country, city, street and house number. How many numbers give the address of an electron in an atom?

secenekler.neden: n gives the shell, ℓ the subshell, mℓ the orbital and ms the spin. So four quantum numbers are needed.
A single number only gives the shell. Many electrons share the same shell.
Two numbers find the subshell, but they do not say which orbital or which electron.

secenekler.neden: Each value of mℓ stands for one orbital. There are three values, so there are three p orbitals.
A single orbital is found in the s subshell. In p, mℓ takes three values.
6 is the most electrons the p subshell can hold. The number of orbitals is 3.

cards.h: Shapes of s, p, d and f orbitals
cards.p: The s orbital is spherical. The p orbitals are dumbbell-shaped, and there are three of them. Most d orbitals look like a four-leaf clover. The s subshell holds 2 electrons, p holds 6, d holds 10 and f holds 14.

once.soru: Which shape is an orbital whose probability is the same in every direction at the same distance from the nucleus?

secenekler.neden: The shape that is the same in every direction is a sphere, which is the s orbital.
A dumbbell-shaped p orbital stretches along one axis. So it is not the same in every direction.
The lobes of clover-shaped d orbitals point in certain directions.

cards.h: Filling order: the n + ℓ rule
cards.p: By the Aufbau principle, an electron goes into the lowest-energy orbital first. The sum n + ℓ sets the order, and the one with the smaller sum fills first. For example, 4s has a sum of 4 and 3d has a sum of 5, so 4s fills first.

cards.p: By the Pauli principle, no two electrons in an atom can have all four quantum numbers the same. Electrons in the same orbital have opposite spins. So an orbital holds at most 2 electrons (↑↓).

once.soru: Two electrons go into one orbital. What must their spins be?

secenekler.neden: Two electrons in the same orbital share n, ℓ and mℓ. All four numbers cannot be the same, so their spins are opposite (↑↓).
Then all four quantum numbers would be the same. That is not allowed.
It does matter, because two electrons with the same spin cannot share an orbital.

cards.p: By Hund's rule, electrons go into orbitals of equal energy one at a time first, all with the same spin. Pairing starts only when every orbital is half full. For example, nitrogen's 2p³ electrons are placed ↑ ↑ ↑.

once.soru: Chlorine (17) has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. What does the sum of the superscripts give?

secenekler.neden: 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17, the number of electrons in neutral chlorine. Each superscript is the number of electrons in that subshell.
The number of shells is the largest value of n, which is 3 here.
A configuration shows only electrons.

cards.p: A long configuration is shortened by writing the symbol of the previous noble gas in square brackets. For example, Na is written [Ne] 3s¹ and Fe [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. The electrons outside the brackets decide the chemical behavior.

once.soru: Sodium (11) has the configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. Its first 10 electrons match neon's (10). How is it written in short?

secenekler.neden: The square brackets stand for neon's 10 electrons in place of 1s² 2s² 2p⁶. What is left is 3s¹.
Argon has 18 electrons, but sodium has only 11.
Helium has 2 electrons. Then 2s² 2p⁶ would be missing.

4s² and 3d¹⁰ are full. There are no unpaired electrons.

once.soru: Nitrogen's three 2p electrons are spread out ↑ ↑ ↑. What happens if you bring nitrogen atoms near a strong magnet?

secenekler.neden: A particle with unpaired electrons is attracted by a magnet. This is called paramagnetic.
Unpaired electrons interact with a magnet.
Weak repulsion is seen in particles whose electrons are all paired.

cards.p:
• An orbital is a region of probability, not a path.
• n gives the shell, ℓ the subshell, mℓ the orientation and ms the spin.
• The subshell with the smaller n + ℓ fills first. An orbital holds at most 2 electrons, and electrons first go in one at a time.
• The ground state is the lowest-energy configuration. Cr and Cu do not follow the rule.

quiz.q: Put each configuration in the right group.
quiz.e: In the ground state, electrons follow the filling order. In an excited state the number of electrons is the same, but one electron has moved up to a higher orbital. There is no 2d subshell, because ℓ can be at most n − 1. 1s³ breaks the Pauli principle.

quiz.q: Put these subshells in filling order using the n + ℓ rule.
quiz.e: The n + ℓ values are 3 for 3s, 4 for 3p, 4 for 4s, 5 for 3d, 5 for 4p and 5 for 5s. When the sums are equal, the one with smaller n fills first. So 3p comes before 4s, 3d before 4p, and 4p before 5s.

quiz.q: How many orbitals are there in total in the n = 3 shell?
quiz.e: For n = 3, ℓ can be 0, 1 or 2, so there are 3s, 3p and 3d subshells. Their orbitals add up to 1 + 3 + 5 = 9.

quiz.q: What is the ground-state configuration of the Cr³⁺ ion of Cr (Z = 24)?
quiz.e: Cr is [Ar] 4s¹ 3d⁵. In the cation, first the 1 electron in 4s (largest n) leaves, then 2 electrons from 3d. The result is [Ar] 3d³, with 21 electrons left.
y: The electron in 4s leaves before those in 3d. In the Cr³⁺ ion, 4s is empty.
Electrons leave 4s first. Also, Cr is 4s¹ 3d⁵, not 4s² 3d⁴.
A cation forms by giving up electrons, not adding them. 24 − 3 = 21 electrons should be left.

periyodik-tablo.title: The periodic table
periyodik-tablo.summary: The periodic table is a map of the elements. An element's place tells you how it behaves.

cards.p: In 1869 Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements by mass and put similar ones in the same column. He left gaps for elements not yet found and predicted their properties. One of them, gallium, was found in 1875.

cards.p: In 1913 Moseley showed that the true order of the elements is their atomic number (number of protons). Today's table is arranged this way and holds 118 elements.

once.soru: Tellurium (127.6) is heavier than iodine (126.9) but comes before it in the table. What is the modern table arranged by?

secenekler.neden: In 1913 Moseley showed that the true order is the number of protons. Te has 52 protons, and I has 53.
If it were arranged by mass, Te and I would swap places.
The table is arranged by the structure of the atom, not by the order of discovery.

cards.p: The horizontal rows of the table are called periods, and there are 7. The period number gives the number of shells. The vertical columns are called groups, and there are 18. Elements in the same main group have similar valence electrons and chemical properties.

cards.p: On the left and in the middle are the metals (shiny, conductive), at the upper right the nonmetals, between them the metalloids, and at the far right the noble gases. Metallic character increases to the left and down.

etk.soru: Put each element in the right group.
ogeler: It sits on the left of the table in 1A, but it is a nonmetal.

once.soru: Chlorine is in group 7A. How many electrons are in its outer shell?

secenekler.neden: The main group number gives the number of valence electrons. An element in group 7A has 7 valence electrons.
Elements in group 1A have 1 valence electron.
17 is chlorine's total number of electrons. Its outer shell has 7.

cards.p: Going down a group, the number of shells increases, so the atom gets bigger. Going right across a period, the number of protons increases, the nucleus pulls the electrons harder, and the atom gets smaller. A cation is smaller than its atom, and an anion is bigger.

cards.key: It increases down a group and decreases to the right. A cation is smaller than its atom, and an anion is bigger than its atom.

cards.p: Ionization energy increases to the right across a period and decreases down a group. There are two exceptions. Going from Be to B and from N to O, the ionization energy drops, because the s² and half-full p³ configurations are more stable.

cards.key: Group 2A has a higher ionization energy than 3A, and 5A higher than 6A. This is because the s² and p³ configurations are spherically symmetric and more stable.

cards.p: As electrons are removed one by one, each one takes more energy. When the valence electrons run out and an inner shell is reached, the energy jumps suddenly. The number of electrons before the jump gives the group number.

once.soru: An atom's successive ionization energies are 738, 1451 and 7733 kJ/mol. How many valence electrons does it have?

secenekler.neden: The first two electrons come off the outer shell easily. The third comes from an inner shell, so the energy jumps. This element, with 2 valence electrons, is magnesium in group 2A.
The third electron comes from an inner shell. So it is not a valence electron.
The second electron also comes off easily. The big jump comes after it.

cards.p: Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls the shared electrons in a bond toward itself. It increases to the right and decreases going down. Fluorine is the most electronegative, and oxygen is second.

once.soru: In the H–F bond, which atom are the shared electrons closer to?

secenekler.neden: Fluorine is the most electronegative element, and it pulls the electrons in the bond toward itself.
Hydrogen pulls much more weakly than fluorine.
Equal sharing happens only between two identical atoms, as in H–H.

cards.p: The energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron is its electron affinity. The highest values are found in the halogens. Nonmetallic character increases to the right and up.

once.soru: Atoms of which group are most eager to gain electrons?

secenekler.neden: When halogens gain one electron, they reach a noble gas configuration. So their electron affinities are the highest.
These are eager to give up electrons, not to gain them.
Noble gases already have a stable configuration. So they are not eager to gain electrons.

cards.h: s, p, d and f blocks
cards.p: The subshell that the last electron enters sets the element's block. 1A, 2A and He are in the s block, and groups 3A–8A are in the p block. The B groups form the d block, and they are called transition metals. The lanthanides and actinides are in the f block.
cards.key: The main groups (A groups) are made of the s and p blocks. The transition metals (B groups) are in the d block.

once.soru: Iron (Fe) is in the B groups in the middle of the table. Which subshell does its last electron enter?

secenekler.neden: Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶, and the last electron enters 3d. The B groups in the middle of the table are the d block.
Elements ending in s are the two groups at the far left of the table.
Elements ending in p are the six groups on the right of the table.

cards.p:
• The modern table is arranged by atomic number and has 7 periods and 18 groups.
• The period number gives the number of shells, and the main group number gives the number of valence electrons.
• Metals are on the left, nonmetals at the upper right and noble gases at the far right.
• Toward the upper right, the radius decreases, and ionization energy and electronegativity usually increase.

quiz.q: Order these from highest to lowest electronegativity. (F: period 2, 7A; Cl: period 3, 7A; S: period 3, 6A; Na: period 3, 1A)
quiz.e: Electronegativity increases to the right and up. F is at the upper right (4.0). Cl is below it (3.2), S is to the left of Cl (2.6), and Na is at the far left of the period (0.9).

quiz.q: Order these isoelectronic ions from largest to smallest radius. (Z: S 16, Cl 17, K 19, Ca 20)
quiz.e: All four particles have 18 electrons. As the number of protons grows, the nucleus pulls the same electrons harder. So S²⁻ with 16 protons is the largest, and Ca²⁺ with 20 protons is the smallest.

quiz.q: A main-group atom has these successive ionization energies (kJ/mol): IE₁ = 578, IE₂ = 1817, IE₃ = 2745, IE₄ = 11 577. How many valence electrons does it have?
quiz.e: The big jump comes from IE₃ to IE₄ (2745 → 11 577). So the first 3 electrons are valence electrons, and the fourth comes from an inner shell. The atom is in group 3A, and it is aluminum.

quiz.q: Which one has the greatest metallic character? (Na: period 3, 1A; K: period 4, 1A; Mg: period 3, 2A; Al: period 3, 3A)
quiz.e: Metallic character increases to the left and down. K is both at the far left (1A) and below Na. Its valence electron is farthest from the nucleus, so it comes off most easily.
y: Na is also in group 1A, but K is below it. Going down, the electron comes off more easily.
Mg is to the right of Na. Metallic character decreases to the right.
Al is the farthest right of these three in period 3. So its metallic character is the smallest.

kimyasal-baglar.title: Interactions between chemical species
kimyasal-baglar.summary: The forces that hold atoms, ions and molecules together.

once.soru: What kind of chemical species is Na⁺?

secenekler.neden: It is a charged sodium particle that has given up one electron.
The neutral atom is Na. The + charge shows that the atom has lost an electron.
A molecule forms when several atoms bond together.

cards.p: Attractions that take more than 40 kJ/mol to break are counted as strong (ionic, covalent, metallic), and those that take less are weak (van der Waals, hydrogen bonds).

once.soru: Which one is a strong interaction?

secenekler.neden: This bond holds atoms together inside a molecule, and breaking it takes a lot of energy.
This interaction is between molecules and counts as weak.
It is a weak attraction between molecules.

once.soru: Neon hardly ever reacts. Why?

secenekler.neden: Neon has 8 electrons in its outer shell. It has no electrons to gain or give up.
It is the outer-shell electrons that decide reactions.
Neon has 10 electrons.

cards.p: A metal gives up electrons and becomes a cation, and a nonmetal gains electrons and becomes an anion. Oppositely charged ions attract each other, and this is called an ionic bond. There are no molecules in NaCl. The ions form a lattice.

cards.h: Formulas and names of ionic compounds
cards.p: In the formula of an ionic compound the charges add up to zero. For example, in Al₂O₃, 2·(+3) + 3·(−2) = 0. A compound is named by saying the cation first and then the anion. NaCl is sodium chloride, and Fe₂O₃ is iron(III) oxide.

cards.key: Single-atom anions end in -ide. Cl⁻ is chloride, O²⁻ oxide, S²⁻ sulfide, F⁻ fluoride and N³⁻ nitride. For metals whose charge can vary, the charge is written as a Roman numeral.

cards.p: In some ions, several atoms carry the charge together. OH⁻ is hydroxide, NO₃⁻ nitrate, SO₄²⁻ sulfate, CO₃²⁻ carbonate and NH₄⁺ ammonium. If more than one of these ions is needed, it goes in parentheses, as in Ca(OH)₂.

once.soru: What is the formula of the compound made of Ca²⁺ and OH⁻ ions?

secenekler.neden: Two OH⁻ are needed to balance the +2 charge. The polyatomic ion goes in parentheses.
Without parentheses the 2 multiplies only H, and there are not two O atoms.
The charges add up to +1, not zero.

cards.p: Nonmetals share their electrons, and both nuclei pull on the shared electron pair. This is called a covalent bond. H₂ has one shared pair, O₂ has two and N₂ has three.

cards.p: In compounds of two nonmetals, the numbers of atoms are given by prefixes: mono, di, tri, tetra, penta and hexa. Mono is not used for the first element. For example, CO is carbon monoxide, and N₂O₅ is dinitrogen pentoxide.

once.soru: What is the name of CO₂?

secenekler.neden: There is one C (mono is not used) and two O (di). So the name is carbon dioxide.
Mono is not used for the first element.
In a compound of two nonmetals, the number of O atoms is given by a prefix.

cards.p: The shared pair shifts toward the more electronegative atom. So the H–Cl bond is polar, and the H–H bond is nonpolar. In symmetrical CO₂ the bond dipoles cancel out. Bent H₂O is a polar molecule.

cards.h: Metallic bonds: a sea of electrons
cards.p: Metal atoms let go of their valence electrons, and these electrons move freely through the metal. The attraction between the cations and this sea of electrons is called a metallic bond. That is why metals conduct and can be hammered into shape.

cards.p: Weak attractions between molecules are called van der Waals forces. Between polar molecules there are dipole–dipole forces, and every molecule has London forces that come from momentary dipoles.

once.soru: At room temperature Cl₂ is a gas and I₂ is a solid. Why do I₂ molecules hold on more tightly?

secenekler.neden: In a big molecule the electrons shift more easily. So the London forces get stronger.
I₂, made of two identical atoms, is nonpolar.

secenekler.yazi: There are ionic bonds between them
secenekler.neden: There are only weak attractions between I₂ molecules.

cards.p: An ion–dipole attraction happens between an ion and a polar molecule. When salt dissolves in water, Na+ pulls on water's δ− oxygen, and Cl− pulls on its δ+ hydrogens.

cards.key: Ions being surrounded by water molecules is called hydration. A polar molecule can create a temporary dipole in a nonpolar molecule, which is called dipole–induced dipole. This is how O₂ dissolves in water, if only a little.

once.soru: When salt dissolves in water, which end of the water molecule does the Na⁺ ion attract?

secenekler.neden: The oxygen end of water has a partial negative (δ−) charge and attracts the positive ion.
The hydrogen end of water is δ+ and repels the Na⁺ ion.
Water is polar, so its ends have different charges.

cards.p: The attraction you just saw is formed only by H bonded to F, O or N. H₂O, NH₃ and HF have hydrogen bonds. CH₄ and H₂S do not.
